title: Thinking with Living Heritage: How Cultural Knowledge Can Strengthen Critical and Systems Thinking
category: Living Heritage, Critical Thinking & Systems Thinking
author: Angga Conni Saputra
excerpt: Living heritage is more than a tradition to preserve. It is a living process of observing, remembering, interpreting, testing, and adapting knowledge across generations. Discover how cultural practices can inspire contextual reasoning, systems thinking, critical inquiry, and more inclusive problem-solving—without romanticising the past.
content:
Living Heritage • Critical Thinking • Systems Thinking

Living heritage is not only something communities inherit and preserve. It is also a living process of observing, remembering, interpreting, testing, and adapting knowledge across generations.

When people hear the word heritage, they may picture monuments, costumes, dances, ceremonies, or objects kept in a museum. Yet much of cultural heritage lives through practice: the way knowledge is taught, a craft is learned, a story is retold, a community organises collective work, or people interpret changes in their environment.

UNESCO uses the term living heritage for intangible cultural heritage that is transmitted between generations and continually recreated in response to communities’ environments, history, and interactions with nature. Its value lies not only in a visible cultural expression, but also in the knowledge, skills, meanings, and relationships carried through it.

That perspective offers an interesting lesson for anyone who wants to think more carefully. Living heritage can help us ask: How do people learn from repeated experience? How do they recognise patterns? How does knowledge change when circumstances change? And how can different kinds of knowledge work together when a community faces a new problem?

Living heritage can be understood not merely as something to know about, but as a way to investigate how knowledge is created, shared, challenged, and adapted.

1. Think in Context, Not in Isolated Facts

A fact rarely explains an entire situation. A practice that makes sense in one place may work differently somewhere else because ecology, livelihoods, history, social relationships, and available resources differ.

For example, imagine a coastal community whose members pay close attention to seasonal winds, tides, cloud formations, or changes in marine life. These observations may have developed through repeated interaction with a particular environment. Their meaning cannot be separated from where they were observed, by whom, and under what circumstances.

A systems thinker asks how those observations connect with fishing practices, household income, local rules, weather patterns, technology, and exposure to risk. Rather than treating a traditional practice as an isolated item, the thinker investigates the relationships that make it meaningful.

Isolated-fact question“What does this community traditionally do?”
Contextual question“Under what conditions did this practice develop, what purpose does it serve, and how is it changing?”
Systems question“Which social, environmental, and economic relationships help explain why the practice works—or no longer works—as expected?”

This way of thinking is useful beyond heritage. Policies, technologies, and management methods also succeed or fail within specific contexts. A solution cannot be evaluated well if we ignore the conditions that shape its results.

2. Look for Patterns Across Time

Living heritage is transmitted through generations, but transmission is not simply the copying of an unchanged instruction. People teach, practise, remember, reinterpret, and adapt. Each generation may preserve some elements while adjusting others in response to new circumstances.

This invites a form of temporal thinking. Instead of asking only what is happening today, we can ask what has changed, what persists, what conditions accompanied earlier changes, and which explanations remain plausible.

In an illustrative coastal example, fishers’ observations might provide clues about how local conditions have varied over time. Those observations should not automatically be treated as a complete forecast. They can instead help generate questions: Have seasonal patterns shifted? Are the observations comparable across years? Have equipment, fishing locations, or reporting practices changed too?

Think critically: a remembered pattern is a valuable lead for inquiry, not automatic proof of a causal relationship. Ask what was observed, how consistently it was observed, what may have changed, and what other evidence is available.

Comparing lived experience with environmental measurements, historical records, or other forms of evidence can produce a richer account than relying on only one source. It also helps prevent us from confusing a pattern that people remember with a pattern that has been independently established.

3. Recognise That Knowledge Is Distributed

No single person necessarily holds all the knowledge needed to understand a complex issue. A craftsperson may understand materials through years of practice. An elder may remember earlier community responses to a crisis. Young people may recognise changing communication habits. Farmers, fishers, performers, healers, educators, and researchers may each contribute different observations, methods, and questions.

These forms of knowledge are not interchangeable, and none should be romanticised. The point is that complex problems often require contributions from people who see different parts of the situation.

Living heritage reminds us to ask not only, “What information do we have?” but also, “Who knows something relevant, how did they learn it, and whose experience is missing from this conversation?”

Experience-based knowledgeWhat people notice through repeated practice, direct observation, and work in a particular setting.
Documented knowledgeWhat is recorded in reports, archives, measurements, research, and formal procedures.
Relational knowledgeWhat becomes visible through trust, dialogue, shared activity, and understanding how people depend on one another.

Good analysis does not ask one form of knowledge to perform every task. It creates a process for comparing contributions, exploring disagreements, and clarifying what each source can and cannot establish.

4. Use Stories and Practices to Generate Better Questions

Stories, sayings, demonstrations, and rituals can carry accumulated interpretations of experience. They can help people remember a warning, communicate a value, or make an abstract relationship easier to discuss. A story can function as a starting model: it points our attention toward a pattern that may deserve closer examination.

But an analogy is not proof. Two situations may look similar while differing in the mechanisms that shape their outcomes. A story about cooperation, for instance, may inspire a team to coordinate better—but the team still needs to examine incentives, roles, resources, and the possibility of disagreement.

A useful thinking sequence is to begin with the cultural expression, identify the idea or relationship it appears to convey, ask where that insight may apply, and then test the comparison against the new context.

Let heritage widen the questions we ask. Let evidence help us judge which answers are defensible.

5. Learn from Practice, Not Only from Explanations

Some knowledge is difficult to communicate fully through a written instruction. Craftsmanship is a clear example: a learner may need to observe a skilled practitioner, handle materials, make mistakes, receive feedback, and repeat a process before developing reliable judgement.

This is not a reason to reject documentation or formal education. It is a reminder that knowing the description of an activity is different from knowing how to perform it under real conditions.

The same distinction appears in professional learning. Reading about stakeholder engagement is not the same as facilitating a difficult discussion. Studying risk management is not the same as responding to an unexpected event. A sound learning design combines explanation with observation, guided practice, reflection, and feedback.

A practical lesson: when a task depends on situated judgement, ask what learners need to observe, practise, discuss, and reflect on—not only what information they need to memorise.

6. Preserve the Capacity to Change

One of the most important features of living heritage is that it can be recreated as communities respond to changing circumstances. Safeguarding a practice therefore does not necessarily mean freezing it in one version or requiring every generation to reproduce it identically.

The same principle matters in thinking. A method that once worked may become less useful when the environment changes. A solution should be understood in relation to the conditions under which it was developed, rather than treated as a universal rule.

At the same time, flexibility should not become an excuse to change a practice without listening to the people who carry it. Communities should be able to participate meaningfully in decisions about how their heritage is documented, transmitted, interpreted, or adapted.

Critical thinking also means recognising that not every inherited practice is automatically fair, safe, or appropriate in every situation. Cultural knowledge deserves serious and respectful engagement, not unquestioning acceptance. Questions of human rights, mutual respect, community agency, and sustainable development matter when considering safeguarding and change.

Two mistakes to avoid: treating tradition as infallible simply because it is old, and dismissing community knowledge simply because it is not expressed in a formal scientific format. Both approaches close down inquiry before it begins.

7. A Practical Method: Think with Living Heritage

The following sequence can help turn cultural knowledge into a respectful and evidence-informed learning process. It is a practical framework, not a universal formula.

Observe the practice in context.
What happens, where does it happen, who participates, and which environmental or social conditions matter?
Listen to the knowledge holders.
Ask participants how the practice is learned, what it means to them, and what changes they have experienced. Do not assume one person speaks for an entire community.
Identify the underlying relationships.
Look for recurring patterns, dependencies, constraints, values, feedback loops, and the problems the practice helps people navigate.
Generate questions, not premature conclusions.
Use stories, observations, and experience to develop hypotheses. Make clear what is known, what is interpreted, and what remains uncertain.
Compare evidence and test the explanation.
Where appropriate, compare accounts with records, measurements, other experiences, or a small practical test. Investigate contradictions rather than hiding them.
Reflect, adapt, and share the learning.
Discuss what the inquiry suggests with the people involved. Consider who benefits, possible unintended consequences, and whether the interpretation respects community agency.

8. Worked Example: Planning a Coastal Learning Activity

Imagine a team preparing a learning activity about coastal environmental change. The team initially plans to deliver a presentation based only on a set of maps and technical slides. The information may be useful, but the team does not yet know whether the material addresses the questions residents consider most important.

A living-heritage-informed approach would not replace environmental science with tradition. It would improve the inquiry by bringing different forms of observation into conversation.

Start with local questionsInvite community members to describe the environmental changes they have noticed, which observations matter to their livelihoods, and what they want the activity to help them decide.
Map different evidenceRecord local observations alongside available maps, measurements, historical records, and expert assessments. Keep the source and uncertainty of each claim visible.
Investigate agreements and gapsAsk which findings support one another, which appear to conflict, and whether differences could be explained by location, timing, measurement, or experience.
Co-design a useful responseDevelop the learning activity with participants, then collect feedback on whether it improves understanding, supports decisions, and responds to the needs they identified.

The benefit is not simply that the activity becomes more culturally engaging. The thinking process itself improves: the team questions its assumptions, widens its evidence base, makes uncertainty visible, and checks whether the intended intervention fits the context.

9. What This Means for Foresight, Education, and Evaluation

For foresight, living heritage can prompt researchers to look beyond formal reports for signs of how people interpret change in everyday life. Stories, skills, social practices, and local observations may raise questions that conventional datasets do not capture. Those signals still need to be assessed for relevance, corroboration, uncertainty, and potential bias.

For education, living heritage can connect learning to familiar practices and relationships. Community-recognised ways of transmitting knowledge can complement formal learning, provided that participation is respectful and the content is developed with those involved.

For monitoring, evaluation, and learning, this perspective encourages us to distinguish between delivering an activity and changing how people understand or respond to a problem. A workshop may be completed successfully without participants gaining greater confidence, using the knowledge, or influencing a decision. Evaluation should therefore examine the mechanism between the activity and the intended outcome.

OutputPeople attended a learning session or a cultural knowledge-sharing activity took place.
Intermediate changeParticipants compare evidence, exchange knowledge, recognise uncertainty, or develop a shared understanding of a problem.
Outcome to investigatePeople use the learning in decisions, adapt a practice where appropriate, or gain a meaningful role in shaping a response.

These outcomes cannot be assumed. They need to be observed and assessed in context, with attention to who participates, whose knowledge is heard, and whether the resulting decisions make a real difference.

10. The Questions Worth Taking Forward

When encountering a cultural practice or a piece of inherited knowledge, try asking:

What problem, relationship, or value does this practice help people understand?
How was the knowledge developed, transmitted, and adapted over time?
Whose experience is represented—and whose perspective may be missing?
What does this knowledge help us notice, and what can it not establish on its own?
How could we test an interpretation while respecting the community and the context?
What should be preserved, what may need to adapt, and who should participate in that decision?

Conclusion: Heritage Can Teach Us How to Think, Not Just What to Remember

Living heritage connects memory with practice, knowledge with relationships, and continuity with change. Approached thoughtfully, it can encourage contextual reasoning, pattern recognition, systems thinking, practical learning, and better questions about whose knowledge informs a decision.

But learning from heritage requires more than admiration. It requires listening, careful interpretation, transparent uncertainty, evidence-informed testing, and respect for the people who sustain the practice. We should neither turn cultural knowledge into a decorative anecdote nor treat it as unquestionable truth.

For me, the deeper lesson is that thinking is not merely the act of collecting information. It is the work of connecting observations, exploring relationships, questioning assumptions, learning from others, and revising our understanding when the context changes.

Living heritage reminds us that knowledge survives not by remaining untouched, but by being meaningfully learned, practised, questioned, and carried forward.

Further Reading

  • UNESCO — What Is Intangible Cultural Heritage?: an overview of living expressions, knowledge, and skills transmitted across generations.
  • UNESCO — Frequently Asked Questions on Living Heritage: explains how living heritage evolves and is recreated in response to changing environments.
  • UNESCO — About Living Heritage and Education: discusses intergenerational transmission and the relationship between living heritage and learning.
  • UNESCO — Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage: the 2003 Convention, including the definition of intangible cultural heritage and safeguarding.

This article proposes a learning framework inspired by the concept of living heritage. The examples are illustrative; any real application should be developed with the relevant communities and supported by context-specific evidence.

title: Opresion vs Consent: When we have the right reason to push the boundary
author: Angga Conni Saputra
excerpt: When change matters, a good reason does not justify every method. Explore why honest persuasion, negotiation, and a willingness to test the outcome are better starting points than deception or coercive control—and why consent, legitimate authority, and proportionality still matter.
content:
Social Change • Persuasion • Consent • Ethics

Sometimes change matters so much that we feel compelled to push people beyond their comfort zones. But having a good reason to seek change does not automatically give us the right to control another person.

In public health, an unreliable reporting process can have serious consequences. If one district runs short of vaccines while another has stock available, fragmented information can make planning and distribution harder. A digital system such as a vaccine logistics application can help—but technology alone does not create change. People also need to understand the system, trust its purpose, and change their working habits.

This raises a difficult question: when we believe a change is necessary, should we compel people to follow it, persuade them, negotiate with them, or offer something that makes the new behaviour worthwhile?

My starting point is simple: if we need someone to change, begin with honest persuasion. Explain the reason, invite questions, negotiate where possible, and try the approach before assuming it will fail.

1. A Good Reason Is Not a Blank Cheque

Consider two situations. In the first, health workers are asked to use a reporting system because accurate stock information supports planning and may help prevent avoidable shortages. The purpose can be explained, the process can be improved, and the results can be checked.

In the second, someone insists that two adults must follow a particular relationship arrangement—for example, that they must date but are not allowed to meet—simply because the person imposing the rule thinks it will make the relationship more exciting. The preference is treated as a command, and questions are seen as disobedience.

Both situations involve an attempt to influence behaviour, but their ethical foundations are very different. One may pursue a legitimate collective objective through an authorised process. The other may simply turn a personal preference into control over someone else's private life.

Ask about the purposeIs the change addressing a real, legitimate problem—or mainly serving the preferences and ego of the person demanding it?
Ask about authorityDoes the person or institution have a legitimate basis to set this requirement? A strong belief alone does not create authority.
Ask about the methodAre the reasons honest? Is the intervention proportionate? Can affected people ask questions or challenge the decision?

Even a legitimate public goal does not justify every method. Equally, a rule that someone dislikes is not automatically oppression. The purpose, authority, process, proportionality, and real-world impact all matter.

2. The Difference Between Persuasion and Coercive Control

Persuasion presents reasons and evidence so that another person can evaluate them. Negotiation allows people to discuss constraints, exchange proposals, and search for a workable agreement. An offer gives someone a choice, provided the terms are transparent and the offer does not disguise an improper threat.

Coercive control is different: it seeks compliance through threats, intimidation, deception, or pressure that seriously undermines a person's ability to choose. Manipulation may also steer a decision by hiding material facts or exploiting a person's vulnerabilities. The categories can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

Visual principle: the quality of an influence attempt is not measured only by whether it gets a “yes.” It also depends on the honesty of the process and whether the person retains meaningful agency.

3. Why Honest Persuasion Is the Best Place to Start

When change is important, it can be tempting to exaggerate the risks, hide uncertainty, or pressure people until they agree. That may create the appearance of success in the short term, but it can damage trust and make it harder to learn what is actually preventing change.

Honest persuasion starts differently. It explains the problem in plain language, shares the best available evidence, acknowledges uncertainty, listens to objections, and gives people a meaningful opportunity to respond. It does not promise that everyone will agree. Its strength is that it treats the other person as someone capable of thinking and deciding.

Explain the reason.
Describe the problem and who may be affected. Do not rely on “because I said so” as the whole argument.
Be truthful about evidence and limits.
Distinguish what is known from what is uncertain. Do not invent urgency, benefits, or consequences to secure agreement.
Listen and negotiate.
Ask what makes the change difficult. Adjust the implementation when reasonable rather than treating every objection as bad faith.
Offer a fair path to try.
Where appropriate, propose a pilot, a trial period, training, practical support, or a clear review point.
Evaluate the result.
Observe what happens. If it works, understand why. If it does not, learn from the evidence and revise the approach instead of escalating pressure automatically.

4. “Let's Try First” Is a Serious Method, Not Indecision

One of the strongest ideas in this approach is to avoid deciding the outcome before the attempt has even been made. We may believe that a new process will work, but the affected people may experience barriers we have not anticipated. A trial can reveal whether the explanation was clear, whether the tools are practical, and whether the proposed change achieves its intended purpose.

In a digital transformation project, for example, low use of an application does not automatically mean that health workers are stubborn or unwilling to change. Connectivity, workload, device access, system design, training, incentives, and trust may all affect adoption. Honest engagement can reveal these barriers and help distinguish a genuine refusal from a system that is difficult to use.

The same principle applies in personal relationships. Explain a preference, hear the other person's view, and discover whether a voluntary agreement is possible. If the other person does not agree, that disagreement is information—not proof that they must be forced to comply.

Try the respectful method, observe what happens, and learn. Do not treat the outcome you want as proof that your preferred method is justified.

5. Consent Is More Than Hearing the Word “Yes”

Consent means more than a person saying yes in a conversation. For consent to be meaningful, the person needs enough relevant information, an adequate understanding of the choice, and a real ability to decline without an improper threat or penalty. The exact requirements depend on the context, but deception and intimidation can undermine freedom to choose.

Persuasion and consent are therefore related, but they are not identical. Persuasion is a way of presenting reasons. Consent is a person's voluntary agreement. Excellent persuasion may result in agreement; it may also result in a thoughtful refusal. Both are possible outcomes of a process that respects agency.

That distinction matters when a person is especially skilled at convincing others. Sales ability, confidence, charisma, or emotional intelligence does not by itself establish whether the influence is ethical. We need to ask whether the claims were truthful, whether relevant information was concealed, whether pressure crossed a line, and whether the other person could realistically say no.

A useful test: would the person still be able to make an informed choice if they knew the relevant facts, understood the consequences, and were free to decline? If not, the apparent agreement deserves closer scrutiny.

6. What About Rules That Really Are Necessary?

Honest persuasion should usually be the first approach when behaviour change is needed, but this does not mean every collective requirement must depend on individual consent. Public services, workplaces, and institutions sometimes need legitimate rules—for example, reporting standards that support essential health logistics.

In those cases, the authority for the rule should be clear, the requirement should be relevant to the objective, and the method of enforcement should be necessary, proportionate, transparent, and accountable. People should know what is required, why it is required, how to comply, and how to raise legitimate concerns.

The key distinction is between a justified, limited requirement and arbitrary domination. A rule is not legitimate merely because someone labels it “for the greater good.” Nor does the existence of a legal power mean every possible use of that power is fair or wise.

In short: use explanation, support, and negotiation wherever they can achieve the needed change. If a formal requirement is genuinely necessary, establish its legitimate basis and apply it with safeguards—not deception or personal domination.

7. Humility: We May Be Right About the Goal and Wrong About the Method

People sometimes become so certain that their goal is correct that they stop examining their own methods. They assume they know what is best for everyone, then treat disagreement as evidence that others are ignorant, disobedient, or morally wrong.

But confidence is not the same as infallibility. We can have good intentions and still misunderstand a situation. We can be right about a problem and wrong about the solution. We can also make a mistake, recognise it, and choose either to repair the harm honestly or to preserve our authority through more pressure and excuses.

When we discover that an earlier decision was wrong, the ethical response is to acknowledge the error, explain what has changed, listen to the people affected, and revise the decision where appropriate. Replacing one imposed story with another does not amount to genuine correction.

For people who approach life through faith, humility can also mean recognising the limits of human judgement instead of treating personal preferences as unquestionable truths. Belief in a good purpose should encourage responsibility and reflection, not become an excuse to dominate other people.

8. A Simple Decision Framework

Is the goal legitimate?
Identify the actual harm or need. Do not confuse a personal preference with a public necessity.
Do I have the authority to require this?
If the answer is unclear, do not assume that conviction gives you the right to decide for someone else.
Have I tried honest persuasion?
Explain, share evidence, invite questions, listen, negotiate, and offer practical support.
Can we test a workable approach?
Where safe and appropriate, agree on a trial, a review date, and what success or failure will look like.
If a rule must be enforced, is it proportionate and accountable?
Use only legitimate, necessary measures. Preserve channels for questions, review, and correction.
Am I respecting the other person's agency?
Do not disguise manipulation as care, or treat a refusal as permission to increase pressure without limit.

Conclusion: Influence Without Pretending to Own Another Person

Social change often requires more than technology or a good policy. It requires people to understand a problem, reconsider familiar habits, and decide whether—and how—to change. Honest persuasion, negotiation, transparent offers, and practical support give that process a stronger ethical foundation.

Sometimes a legitimate rule is necessary. But we should not jump to compulsion just because we are convinced that we are right. We should first explain the reason, try a respectful approach, observe the result, and learn. Where authority to require a change exists, its use must still be limited and accountable.

Start with honesty. Persuade before you pressure. Try before you assume. And remember: wanting someone to change does not mean you own the right to control their life.

Further Reading

  • Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: a scholarly starting point for exploring philosophical questions about freedom, autonomy, and coercion.
  • World Health Organization — Health Systems Governance: background on governance and decision-making in health systems.
  • UNESCO — Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights: principles concerning human dignity, autonomy, consent, and responsibility in bioethics.

This article offers a conceptual framework, not legal advice. Whether a particular requirement is lawful or justified depends on its context, applicable rules, and the rights of the people affected.

title: Are We Becoming Dumber? The Cognitive Shift Behind Modern Idiocracy
author: Angga Conni Saputra
excerpt: Are people becoming less intelligent, or are modern systems rewarding fragmented thinking? An analytical exploration of education, specialisation, information overload, political incentives, systems thinking, and the proposed M-shaped approach to connecting multiple areas of expertise.
content:
Social Change • Education • Cognition • Systems Thinking

Are people actually becoming less intelligent—or are modern systems making fragmented thinking more visible, more profitable, and more consequential?

There is a familiar cultural image for this question: Idiocracy, the 2006 satirical film in which a society appears to have drifted into collective stupidity. Its exaggerated world is funny precisely because some of its patterns feel uncomfortably recognisable: public debate reduced to slogans, institutions rewarded for spectacle, and complex problems answered with embarrassingly simple solutions.

Look at public discourse today—including the statements of some politicians, executives, commentators, and online influencers—and a similar question may arise: Why does so much public reasoning sometimes look shallow? Are people less intelligent? Has IQ declined? Or are we confusing the ability to solve a narrow problem with the ability to understand a wider system?

My argument is not that modern people are universally becoming stupid. That would be too broad a claim for the available evidence. Instead, I propose a more useful question: could changes in education, work, information environments, incentives, and everyday habits be encouraging forms of thinking that are highly specialised but poorly integrated?

The problem may not always be a lack of intelligence. It may be a mismatch between the complexity of the world and the way we are trained, rewarded, and equipped to think about it.

1. Before Calling Anyone “Dumb,” Ask What Shapes Human Thinking

Thinking does not develop in isolation. It is shaped by biology, health, family life, language, education, culture, economic pressure, workplace design, technology, and the incentives surrounding a decision. These factors do not determine every individual's thinking, but they influence which habits are practised, which questions feel safe to ask, and which kinds of reasoning receive rewards.

EducationWhat do learners practise: recalling approved answers, or questioning assumptions, comparing explanations, and transferring knowledge to unfamiliar problems?
Work and institutionsAre people rewarded for understanding the whole problem—or only for hitting a target inside their own department?
Information environmentsDoes a person encounter context and competing evidence, or a stream of short, emotionally charged fragments?
Tools and technologyDo tools extend human reasoning, or are they used in ways that encourage people to accept outputs without checking them?
Stress and scarcityWhen time, money, sleep, or psychological safety is limited, how much room remains for reflection and complex reasoning?
Social incentivesIs changing one's mind treated as learning—or as weakness, betrayal, or loss of status?

These are interacting influences, not a ranked list of proven causes of societal decline. The same educational system can nurture curiosity in one classroom and rote compliance in another. The same technology can support a researcher who verifies sources and mislead a user who accepts every fluent answer. Context matters.

2. Is IQ Declining? The Evidence Is More Complicated Than a Meme

IQ is not a complete measure of human worth, wisdom, judgement, creativity, moral character, or practical competence. It measures performance on particular cognitive tasks under particular testing conditions. It can be informative, but it does not directly tell us whether someone understands institutions, recognises a feedback loop, navigates a conflict ethically, or makes a sound political decision.

Research on generational IQ-test performance illustrates why sweeping claims are risky. The Flynn effect describes substantial rises in average intelligence-test scores across many populations during much of the twentieth century. Later research also found that these gains slowed or reversed in some countries and cohorts. For example, a Norwegian study using conscription records found a rise and later decline in test scores within the same family lineages, supporting an important role for environmental factors rather than a simple story about changing parental composition. These findings do not establish that everyone is getting smarter or dumber everywhere; results vary by place, period, test, and cognitive domain.

The careful conclusion is therefore narrower: IQ trends are real research questions, but a film, a political speech, a viral post, or a frustrating meeting cannot diagnose population intelligence. We need representative data and clear definitions—not impressions alone.

Important distinction: “This person made a poor argument” is an observation about an argument. “This person has low IQ” is a claim about a person's cognitive ability. The first does not prove the second.

3. Education: Are We Teaching People to Think, or Mainly to Reproduce Answers?

Education is one of the first places to examine—not because schools everywhere fail, but because education shapes habits of attention and reasoning at scale. A learner can memorise a definition, reproduce a formula, pass an examination, and still struggle to apply the knowledge to a different setting. Knowledge acquisition and knowledge transfer are related, but they are not identical.

Consider a student who learns the definition of supply and demand. The student may correctly explain a textbook graph. But can they connect a fuel subsidy to price signals, state expenditure, transport costs, household behaviour, and possible unintended consequences? Can they distinguish a short-term relief measure from a long-term structural policy? That requires moving between concepts and analysing relationships, not merely remembering one concept well.

OECD reporting on PISA 2022 learning strategies offers a useful, limited illustration. Across OECD countries, fewer than 60% of students reported using critical-thinking or perspective-taking strategies, and fewer than half reported regularly connecting newly learned material to what they already knew during mathematics lessons. These are self-reported strategies in a specific educational context—not proof that young people are unintelligent. They do, however, point to the importance of actively teaching learners how to question, connect, and transfer knowledge.

Higher education deserves scrutiny too. An OECD comparative study of critical-thinking assessment across six higher-education systems found that students' average performance improved between entry and exit, but the measured gain was relatively small. The report also cautions that a degree is not, by itself, a reliable guarantee of generic skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, analytic reasoning, and communication.

The practical question for education is not simply, “How much content did the learner cover?” It is also: What can the learner do with that knowledge when the problem changes?

RecallCan I state the concept or reproduce the method?
ApplicationCan I use it in a familiar practical situation?
TransferCan I recognise when it applies to a different situation?
IntegrationCan I connect it to other variables, competing explanations, and long-term consequences?

4. Specialisation: Deep Knowledge Can Coexist With a Narrow View

Modern economies depend on specialisation. We need people who know medicine, engineering, law, economics, education, cybersecurity, logistics, and countless other fields in depth. Specialisation allows societies to develop knowledge that no individual could master in full.

The risk appears when specialisation turns into intellectual isolation. A specialist may understand one component exceptionally well but lack the vocabulary, incentive, or opportunity to consider what happens at the boundaries between components. This is not necessarily personal failure. Organisations often divide work into departments, allocate budgets by function, measure employees through narrow indicators, and schedule so little shared reflection that the whole problem becomes nobody's responsibility.

Imagine a city transport agency. One team is rewarded for reducing operating costs, another for keeping vehicles moving, and another for meeting passenger-service targets. Each team may hit its own KPI while the overall system becomes less reliable: maintenance gets postponed, passenger transfers become worse, and costs are merely shifted elsewhere. The local numbers can look good while the public outcome deteriorates.

This is a classic systems problem: optimising a part does not always optimise the whole. What looks like stupidity from outside may sometimes be a predictable result of fragmented responsibility and badly aligned incentives. That explanation does not remove accountability; it helps identify what actually needs to change.

A system can be full of capable people and still produce an outcome that nobody would have chosen if they had understood the whole system.

5. Linear Thinking Is Useful—Until the Problem Stops Being Linear

Linear thinking is not inherently inferior. Step-by-step reasoning is indispensable for calculations, procedures, troubleshooting, and tasks where a clear sequence is appropriate. The problem is treating every problem as if it had one cause, one solution, and one predictable consequence.

Complex public problems rarely work that way. Housing, education, public health, climate adaptation, poverty, and political trust involve interacting variables, delayed effects, feedback loops, competing goals, and uncertainty. A policy can solve one immediate problem while creating another later. A successful intervention in one community may not transfer unchanged to another community with different institutions and incentives.

Systems thinking adds several questions to the conventional “What should we do?”

What else influences this outcome?
Look beyond the most visible or politically convenient cause. Ask which social, economic, technical, and institutional variables matter.
What changes because of our intervention?
People adapt. Incentives shift. A rule may produce workarounds, unintended consequences, or new pressures elsewhere.
What happens over time?
Separate immediate effects from delayed effects. Short-term success can conceal long-term costs.
Where is the boundary of our analysis?
Ask which actors, communities, costs, and consequences are missing from the picture.

Donella Meadows' work on systems and leverage points is a useful introduction to the idea that changing a system's rules, information flows, goals, or underlying assumptions may matter more than tweaking a visible parameter. The wider lesson is intellectual humility: a solution should be judged by the behaviour of the whole system, not by the elegance of its slogan.

6. Information Overload, Attention, and Cognitive Offloading

Our information environment has changed dramatically. Many people now encounter news, commentary, advertising, entertainment, work messages, and algorithmically recommended content through the same devices. The issue is not simply that there is “too much information.” It is that information arrives at different speeds, with different levels of credibility, context, and emotional intensity.

Short-form content can be useful: it introduces unfamiliar topics and makes ideas accessible. But fragments can also remove the conditions needed for careful judgement. A 20-second clip may show a politician saying something outrageous while omitting the question, previous exchange, policy details, or later clarification. A chart can be technically accurate yet misleading when its time window, denominator, or comparison group is hidden. Repetition may create familiarity without establishing truth.

Digital tools also change how we remember and reason. Cognitive scientists use the term cognitive offloading for strategies that shift some mental work onto the environment—for example, writing a reminder, using a calculator, or asking a search engine to retrieve a fact. Offloading can be adaptive; nobody should need to memorise everything. But a tool's convenience can become a liability when people stop checking what it has returned, forget how to evaluate it, or outsource the judgement rather than just the memory task.

AI makes this tension more visible. It can help compare perspectives, summarise long material, generate hypotheses, and identify relationships a user might miss. It can also produce fluent but false claims. The productive question is not “Should we use tools?” It is: Which parts of thinking should we delegate, and which parts must remain under human scrutiny?

A useful rule: outsource retrieval and routine operations when appropriate; retain responsibility for framing the question, checking evidence, examining assumptions, and deciding what the result means.

7. Why Politicians and Public Institutions Can Look Irrational

Political communication is an especially revealing case because elected officials often speak under competing pressures: they need to persuade supporters, survive news cycles, negotiate with allies, respond to crises, and appear decisive. A complete explanation may be intellectually honest but difficult to compress into a memorable message. A slogan may travel further than a qualified analysis.

Several mechanisms can make public reasoning look shallow: strategic simplification, short electoral horizons, party discipline, reward for attention, selective use of evidence, motivated reasoning, and weak feedback between a policy decision and the people experiencing its consequences. In some cases, the problem may be a lack of knowledge or poor judgement. In others, the speaker may understand the complexity but choose not to communicate it—or may be responding rationally to incentives that produce socially damaging outcomes.

That is why we should be careful about inferring IQ from a politician's public performance. A person can be intellectually capable and still behave opportunistically. A person can be confident and still be wrong. A person can be technically correct about one detail and misunderstand the wider consequences. These are different failures and require different remedies.

Explaining incentives is not the same as excusing misconduct. Leaders remain accountable for claims, decisions, and consequences. But if the same shallow behaviour repeatedly emerges across different people, the institutional design deserves scrutiny as well as the individual.

8. An Interactive Model: Which Conditions Are Shaping the Thinking?

The diagram below is a conceptual map, not a causal model estimated from data. Select a lens to highlight how one set of conditions may influence thinking habits. In real life, the pathways overlap and can reinforce one another.

Choose a lens to highlight a pathway
Education lens: Learners practise the habits that classrooms measure. A system that rewards recall alone may develop recall efficiently; adding questioning, comparison, explanation, and transfer gives learners practice at connecting ideas.
Work and institutions lens: Targets and departmental boundaries shape attention. If every unit optimises a local metric, someone must still examine cross-department consequences and the overall public outcome.
Information and tools lens: Search, feeds, and AI can extend cognition. The key safeguard is to keep source-checking, context reconstruction, and judgement in the workflow.
Human conditions lens: Complex reasoning requires some capacity for attention and reflection. Chronic stress, poor sleep, overload, or fear of speaking up can make careful thinking harder without saying anything definitive about a person's underlying intelligence.

Conceptual illustration by the author. The arrows represent plausible influences, not measured effect sizes or proof that every pathway operates in every person.

9. From T-Shaped Skills to M-Shaped Thinking

Professional development often uses the metaphor of T-shaped skills: the vertical stroke represents depth in one domain, while the horizontal stroke represents breadth across other domains. UNESCO-UNEVOC's TVETipedia glossary describes the model in terms of deep ability combined with broader knowledge and experience across domains.

For the argument developed here, I propose M-shaped thinking as a useful metaphor. Imagine more than one vertical pillar of depth, connected by a horizontal ability to move between domains and relate them to a wider system. The aim is not to become an expert in everything. It is to cultivate several meaningful areas of depth, enough cross-domain literacy to communicate with other specialists, and the habit of asking how the pieces interact.

Important terminology note: “M-shaped thinking” is used here as an authorial framework, not presented as a universally standardised scientific construct with one agreed definition or validated measurement scale. Its value should be judged by whether it helps people describe and practise a useful set of skills—not by the shape of the letter alone.

DepthKnow a field well enough to evaluate its methods, limitations, and evidence.
Additional depthBuild competence in another field or method that complements the first, rather than collecting superficial buzzwords.
BridgesDevelop vocabulary and curiosity that help you collaborate across disciplines.
Systems viewAsk how variables, incentives, institutions, people, and time interact—and revise your model when evidence changes.

M-shaped thinking is therefore not a rejection of specialisation. It is a proposal for making specialisation more connected. A public-policy professional might combine policy analysis, monitoring and evaluation, and digital systems; a public-health specialist might connect clinical knowledge, logistics, behavioural science, and data; an engineer might integrate technical design, safety, economics, and environmental impact. The point is not to claim mastery of all these domains, but to understand enough of their relationships to ask better questions.

10. How to Practise M-Shaped Thinking Without Becoming a Superficial Generalist

Keep one area of real depth.
Build a strong core of knowledge and methods. Breadth without depth can turn into confident but shallow generalisation.
Add a complementary discipline.
Choose a field that explains something your core field routinely struggles with—for example, behavioural science alongside policy, or data literacy alongside programme management.
Learn the limits of each discipline.
Ask what counts as evidence, what assumptions a method makes, and what it cannot tell you.
Practise explaining one problem through multiple lenses.
Describe it economically, socially, institutionally, technically, and ethically. Then identify where the explanations agree or conflict.
Draw causal maps before recommending solutions.
List major variables, possible feedback loops, affected groups, time delays, and unintended consequences. Mark uncertainty instead of pretending every link is proven.
Work with people who know what you do not.
Interdisciplinary thinking is not solitary omniscience. It depends on asking specialists good questions and respecting evidence outside one's expertise.
Review outcomes, not just intentions.
Compare the predicted outcome with what actually happened. A useful thinker updates the model when the world disagrees.

Organisations can support these habits by rewarding cross-functional outcomes, creating space for constructive disagreement, sharing data across boundaries, and reviewing whether indicators are distorting behaviour. Training a staff member to think critically will not solve an institutional problem if the organisation punishes them for raising inconvenient evidence.

11. A Practical Test: Is This a Knowledge Gap, a Reasoning Gap, or a System Problem?

When someone makes a poor decision, avoid jumping immediately to a character judgement. Ask what kind of failure you are observing. The categories below overlap, but distinguishing them helps determine the response.

Knowledge gapThe person lacks a relevant fact or concept. Response: teach, explain, provide reliable information, and check understanding.
Reasoning gapThe information is available, but the person draws an invalid conclusion, ignores a counterexample, or fails to compare alternatives. Response: examine the argument and practise reasoning.
Integration gapThe person understands individual pieces but fails to connect them across domains, time horizons, or affected groups. Response: map relationships and feedback.
Incentive problemThe person or organisation is rewarded for an action that harms the wider outcome. Response: redesign the incentives and accountability—not just the training.
Information problemThe evidence is incomplete, misleading, inaccessible, or stripped of context. Response: improve provenance, transparency, and verification.
Capacity or safety problemTime pressure, overload, fatigue, fear, or lack of resources makes reflection difficult. Response: improve working conditions and psychological safety where possible.

This framework avoids two mistakes. The first is blaming individuals for failures produced by the system around them. The second is blaming “the system” so broadly that nobody is held accountable for choices they could reasonably have made differently.

12. A Short Self-Audit for Complex Thinking

Use these questions before making a confident judgement about a person, policy, or public controversy. They are not an IQ test. They are prompts for checking the quality of your own reasoning.

1. What do I know directly, and what am I merely assuming?

2. What evidence would change my mind?

3. Which variables or affected groups are missing from my explanation?

4. Am I confusing a visible symptom with the underlying cause?

5. What incentives could make a capable person behave this way?

6. What second-order or long-term consequence might follow my proposed solution?

7. Have I checked the original source, context, timeframe, and denominator behind a claim?

8. Can I explain the strongest reasonable alternative view without caricaturing it?

Conclusion: Perhaps the Crisis Is Not Stupidity, but Fragmentation

Idiocracy offers a comic image of collective decline. Real societies are more complicated. Intelligence-test trends vary; education systems have different strengths and weaknesses; digital tools can help or hinder; and political behaviour reflects a mixture of capability, incentives, identity, institutions, and choice. There is no responsible basis for reducing all of this to “everyone is becoming dumb.”

Yet the concern beneath the joke is worth taking seriously. We can produce highly educated specialists who struggle to transfer their knowledge, institutions that reward local success while neglecting collective outcomes, and public conversations that reward speed and certainty more than careful explanation. Such outcomes can look like stupidity even when the underlying problem is more structural.

The answer is not to abandon expertise, romanticise the past, or demand that everyone become an expert in everything. It is to connect depth with breadth, evidence with context, and individual competence with systems understanding. Education should cultivate questioning and transfer; organisations should align incentives with whole-system outcomes; technology should support verification rather than replace judgement; and public leaders should be evaluated on the quality and consequences of their reasoning—not merely their confidence or performance.

Maybe the modern challenge is not that people have stopped thinking. It is that many systems train them to think deeply about one slice of reality while giving them too little practice in seeing how the slices fit together.

That is the case for M-shaped thinking: not an official diagnosis of society, but a practical invitation to build multiple areas of depth, connect them responsibly, and learn to see beyond the boundaries of our own expertise.

Further Reading and Research

  • Bratsberg & Rogeberg (2018), “Flynn effect and its reversal are both environmentally caused,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. A large Norwegian conscription-record study on rising and later declining cognitive test scores, including within-family analyses.
  • Pietschnig & Voracek (2015), “The Flynn Effect: A Meta-analysis,” Perspectives on Psychological Science. A meta-analysis of historical changes in IQ test scores and the interpretive challenges involved.
  • OECD, PISA 2022 Results, Volume V: Learning Strategies. Findings on critical-thinking strategies, perspective-taking, connecting new and prior knowledge, motivation, and learning environments.
  • OECD (2022), “Does Higher Education Teach Students to Think Critically?” Comparative assessment and discussion of critical thinking and other generic academic skills in higher education.
  • UNESCO-UNEVOC TVETipedia: “T-shaped skills.” A concise glossary definition of depth in one domain combined with breadth across domains.
  • The Donella Meadows Project: “A Visual Approach to Leverage Points.” An accessible introduction to systems thinking and interventions that can change system behaviour.
  • Risko & Gilbert (2016), “Cognitive Offloading,” Trends in Cognitive Sciences. A review of how people use external tools and environments to reduce internal cognitive demands.

Scope note: This article is an analytical argument and conceptual framework, not a claim that all people are less intelligent, a clinical assessment, or a validated measurement of “M-shaped thinking.” Empirical findings cited above concern specific populations, measures, and periods; they should not be generalised beyond what those studies support.
