content:
Psychology · Adaptive Thinking · Problem Solving

Goal-Oriented Thinking: Stop Worshipping the Method, Start Focusing on the Goal

Some people call me adaptable. Others might call me indecisive, inconsistent, or even ababil—someone who keeps changing their mind. Fair enough. Sometimes I do change my plans. But there is something I genuinely struggle to understand: why do some people abandon their entire goal when just one particular method becomes unavailable?

Article 84 · By Angga Conni Saputra · October 27, 2026

Different routes. Different methods. One destination.

1. A Simple Trip to Bandung

Imagine this.

You have planned a trip to Bandung. You have already taken time off work and booked a hotel. Everything is ready.

There is just one problem: your new motorcycle's registration document, the STNK, has not been issued yet.

What would you do?

Personally, I would look for another reasonable option. Use another roadworthy and legally compliant motorcycle. Take the train. Take a bus. Depending on the circumstances, perhaps even walk for part of the journey.

Why cancel an entire trip when the original vehicle is unavailable?

Of course, walking all the way to Bandung may be impractical, and not every alternative is safe, affordable, or feasible. The point is not that every method is interchangeable. The point is that we should evaluate alternatives against the actual goal and its real constraints.

Now imagine someone saying:

"If I cannot go with my new motorcycle, I am not going at all."

That might make sense if the purpose of the trip is specifically to test the new motorcycle. But if the purpose is to enjoy a holiday in Bandung, the motorcycle is a means—not the destination.

And that distinction changes everything.

2. Goal-Oriented vs. Method-Focused Thinking

The difference is not about being careless with plans. It is about distinguishing the destination from the route.

A goal-oriented person asks, "What am I actually trying to achieve, and what other viable routes could get me there?"

A method-focused person may instead ask, "How can I make this one particular plan work?" Even when that plan is no longer viable.

Planning is valuable. Standards matter. Procedures can protect people and ensure quality. But when we confuse a preferred method with the underlying objective, a useful plan can become an unnecessary obstacle.

3. Why Do People Become Attached to One Method?

Psychology offers several useful concepts for understanding this behaviour. They are possible explanations, not diagnoses of any particular person.

01. Cognitive rigidity

The tendency to persist with an established way of thinking or behaving, even when circumstances change. Generating or accepting alternatives can become difficult.

02. Need for cognitive closure

Some people strongly prefer certainty, predictability, order, and definite answers. An established plan can feel reassuring, while ambiguity and last-minute changes can feel uncomfortable.

03. Functional fixedness

We may see an object or resource only in its familiar role. More broadly, we can become mentally attached to one way of using a tool or solving a problem and overlook other possibilities.

04. Sunk-cost thinking

After investing time, money, or effort in a plan, people can feel compelled to stick with it. Past investment, however, does not automatically make continuing the best decision.

Need for cognitive closure: certainty can feel safer than flexibility

In their influential 1996 paper, Arie W. Kruglanski and Donna M. Webster described the need for cognitive closure through two tendencies: seizing on an answer and freezing on it. In everyday terms, a person may settle on a decision quickly and then resist reopening it when new information appears.

Imagine someone who has mentally committed to a trip on a new motorcycle. When the STNK is delayed, they may experience the change not as a small logistical problem, but as a disruption to the certainty and structure of their plan.

This concept does not mean that everyone who prefers a fixed plan has a high need for closure. Research describes tendencies and contexts, not a simple label that can explain every individual.

Research: Kruglanski & Webster (1996), Motivated Closing of the Mind: “Seizing” and “Freezing,” Psychological Review.

Cognitive rigidity: when the plan survives but the purpose disappears

A 2002 review by Wesley Schultz and Alan Searleman examined a century of research on rigidity in thought and behaviour. Rigidity is a broad, multidimensional construct; it can involve persisting with familiar mental or behavioural patterns.

In practical problem-solving, the warning sign is not simply having a preference. It is failing to reconsider that preference when the conditions that justified it have changed.

Research: Schultz & Searleman (2002), Rigidity of Thought and Behavior: 100 Years of Research.

Functional fixedness: seeing only one possible route

Research on human planning also explores why people can display conceptual inflexibility even when they are capable of planning flexibly. A 2023 paper by Mark K. Ho, Jonathan D. Cohen, and Thomas L. Griffiths examines rational simplification and rigidity in human planning, including the problem of functional fixedness.

In our example, the person may not literally believe that no other transport exists. They may simply be so focused on the original arrangement that alternatives never become serious candidates.

Research: Ho, Cohen & Griffiths (2023), Rational Simplification and Rigidity in Human Planning, Psychological Science.

4. Being Adaptable Does Not Mean Having No Principles

There is an important distinction here. I am not arguing that we should abandon every rule, standard, or commitment whenever something becomes inconvenient.

Some requirements are essential. A vehicle must be legal and safe. A project may require a specific technical standard. A medical procedure may have non-negotiable safety requirements. In those cases, the constraint is part of what makes the goal legitimate or achievable.

The better question is:

Is this requirement essential to the outcome, or is it simply my preferred way of getting there?

Keep the essentials

Safety, legality, ethics, quality, budget limits, and any genuinely mandatory requirements.

Reconsider the preferences

The original vehicle, familiar workflow, favourite software, preferred schedule, or the first solution that came to mind.

Adaptability is not random change. It is the ability to preserve what matters while reconsidering what can change.

5. The Same Principle Applies at Work

Think about a project that depends on one software platform. The platform becomes unavailable. Do we stop the entire project immediately, or do we evaluate a safe alternative that can still meet the requirements?

Think about an event that requires a particular room. The room becomes unavailable. Is the event itself impossible, or could a different venue serve the same purpose?

Think about a team that insists on following an old process simply because it has always been done that way. If the process no longer serves the objective, should we preserve it unquestioningly—or review it against the outcome we need?

In each case, the same sequence helps:

1. Define the outcome. What does success actually mean?

2. Identify the real constraints. What must remain true for the result to be safe, ethical, valid, and useful?

3. Separate requirements from preferences. Which parts of the plan are essential, and which are replaceable?

4. Generate alternatives. What other routes could satisfy the same constraints?

5. Evaluate and adapt. Choose a feasible alternative, or revise the goal transparently if no viable option exists.

This is not an argument against planning. It is an argument for planning that remains responsive to reality.

6. A Small Question That Can Change the Way We Think

When a plan fails, pause before declaring the entire mission impossible.

Ask yourself:

  • What was the original goal?
  • Why did I choose this method in the first place?
  • Has the method become impossible, or merely inconvenient?
  • Can another method meet the essential requirements?
  • Am I protecting the outcome—or protecting my attachment to the plan?

That final question is especially useful. Sometimes we defend a method because it is genuinely the best option. Other times, we defend it because we have already imagined success in one particular form.

Knowing the difference takes reflection, not just flexibility.

My takeaway:

Be committed to your goal, but flexible with your method.

If you want to reach Bandung, let's discuss the best feasible way to get there. Walking, taking a train, boarding a bus, or riding a different motorcycle may all be worth considering, depending on the circumstances.

But if the only acceptable outcome is to use one particular motorcycle, ask yourself whether reaching Bandung was ever the real goal—or whether the motorcycle was the goal all along.

Maybe I am adaptable. Maybe someone else would call that inconsistent. But I would rather reconsider a method and achieve a meaningful outcome than preserve a perfect plan that leads nowhere.

What do you think? Have you ever seen a project, trip, or opportunity fail simply because people insisted on one particular way of doing things?

References

  1. Kruglanski, A. W., & Webster, D. M. (1996). Motivated Closing of the Mind: “Seizing” and “Freezing.” Psychological Review, 103(2), 263–283.
  2. Schultz, P. W., & Searleman, A. (2002). Rigidity of Thought and Behavior: 100 Years of Research. Genetic, Social, and General Psychology Monographs, 128(2), 165–207.
  3. Ho, M. K., Cohen, J. D., & Griffiths, T. L. (2023). Rational Simplification and Rigidity in Human Planning. Psychological Science, 34(11), 1281–1292.

This article discusses possible psychological mechanisms for everyday behaviour. These concepts are not diagnoses, and a person's reasons for preferring a particular method depend on context.

title: How to Become a Modern-Day Great Sage: Cultivating the Mind in the Age of Information Overload
author: Angga Conni Saputra
excerpt: What if the Great Sage was not simply someone who emptied the mind and waited for enlightenment, but someone who deliberately cultivated attention, knowledge, emotional discipline, and practical skill? A modern framework for becoming a lifelong learner in an age of information overload.
content:
Living Heritage · Cognitive Development · Lifelong Learning

How to Become a Modern-Day Great Sage

What if the Great Sage was not simply someone who emptied the mind and waited for enlightenment? What if the ancient image of the hermit, the cultivator, and the scholar described a disciplined process of developing the mind—reducing distractions, studying deeply, training deliberately, and learning to act with wisdom?

Article 85 · By Angga Conni Saputra · October 28, 2026

Ancient metaphors. Modern lessons. A wiser way to learn.

1. The Hypothesis: Perhaps the Sage Was Cultivating More Than Stillness

In stories about ancient sages, we often encounter a familiar scene: a person retreats to a mountain, leaves behind ordinary distractions, meditates, reads scrolls, practices for years, and eventually acquires extraordinary knowledge or insight.

One interpretation focuses on emptiness: the sage clears the mind, abandons worldly desires, and waits for enlightenment or guidance to arrive. That may capture part of the meaning in some spiritual traditions, but it does not tell the whole story of the metaphor.

Here is an alternative hypothesis—not a claim that every ancient tradition meant exactly this, but a modern interpretation worth exploring:

Perhaps the Great Sage is not someone who empties the mind of knowledge, but someone who clears away what prevents the mind from learning.

Under this interpretation, retreat is not the final destination. It is a method for reclaiming attention. Emotional discipline is not the rejection of human feeling. It is the ability to feel without being controlled by every impulse. Reading scrolls is not decorative storytelling. It represents the deliberate acquisition of knowledge. Cultivation is the repeated practice that turns knowledge into capability.

The metaphor becomes surprisingly contemporary when we consider our current environment: endless notifications, fragmented attention, algorithmic feeds, emotionally provocative content, and a constant supply of information that is easy to consume but not always easy to understand or remember.

We might call some of this brainrot or information overload. These terms should not be treated as clinical diagnoses, and digital media is not inherently harmful. The central concern is whether our habits leave enough time and attention for reflection, sustained learning, and meaningful practice.

The Great Sage Hypothesis: A modern sage deliberately protects attention, reduces unproductive mental noise, develops emotional self-regulation, studies reliable sources, practices useful skills, tests assumptions, and integrates what they learn into sound judgment.

This is a working framework inspired by ancient metaphors and informed by modern learning research. It is not a historical claim about the original meaning of every sage, hermit, or cultivator in every culture.

2. Four Metaphors, One Developmental Path

The four stages are a practical interpretation of the metaphors—not a universal historical doctrine.

1. The Hermit: protect attention

Reduce avoidable distractions and create periods for focused thought. The aim is not social isolation; it is intentional control over where attention goes.

2. The Cultivator: practice

Choose abilities worth developing, work on specific weaknesses, seek feedback, and repeat the practice. Exposure alone is not mastery.

3. The Scholar: understand

Read, compare sources, ask why, identify uncertainty, retrieve ideas from memory, and explain concepts in your own words.

4. The Great Sage: integrate

Use knowledge with judgment. Consider context, trade-offs, ethics, uncertainty, and consequences before deciding what to do.

3. First Principle: Clear the Noise, Not the Mind

The phrase “empty your mind” can be misunderstood as a call to stop thinking. For this framework, a more useful interpretation is to reduce the dominance of mental habits that repeatedly hijack attention.

Jealousy, envy, anger, resentment, anxiety, and desire are normal human experiences. The goal is not to erase emotions or pretend that nothing matters. Emotions can provide important signals. The task is to notice them, understand what they are telling us, and avoid letting a passing impulse make every decision.

Try a simple three-question pause when a strong emotion appears:

  1. What am I feeling? Name the emotion without immediately judging yourself.
  2. What triggered it? Separate observable facts from assumptions and interpretations.
  3. What response serves my values and goals? Choose a response rather than automatically obeying the first impulse.

Attention also needs protection from the environment. Put the phone out of reach during a focused learning session, turn off non-essential notifications, and decide in advance what you intend to learn before opening a feed or browser.

Practical rule: Do not ask only, “How much information did I consume today?” Ask, “What can I now explain, remember, evaluate, or do that I could not do before?”

This is not a claim that all entertainment or social media degrades cognition. Digital tools can teach, connect, and inspire. The key is whether use is deliberate and balanced, or whether it repeatedly displaces the activities you value.

4. Second Principle: Train Both Divergent and Convergent Thinking

A modern Great Sage needs more than a large collection of facts. Complex problems often require two complementary modes of thinking.

Divergent thinking generates a range of possible ideas, interpretations, or solutions. It asks: What else could be true? What alternatives have I overlooked? How might this problem be approached differently?

Convergent thinking evaluates and narrows those possibilities. It asks: Which options fit the evidence? What constraints matter? What are the costs, risks, and trade-offs? Which choice is most defensible?

These modes are not enemies, and they are not necessarily separate stages that occur only once. Creative work often alternates between generating ideas, evaluating them, discovering gaps, and returning to exploration. Research reviews also suggest that divergent thinking draws on multiple executive processes, including flexible attention and working memory; the exact relationships are complex and not fully settled.

Further reading: Divergent thinking and the core executive functions: a state-of-the-art review (2022); Metacontrol of human creativity: the neurocognitive mechanisms of convergent and divergent thinking (2020); and the OECD discussion of divergent and convergent thinking.

Try Invergent: a deliberate thinking workout

If you want to practice switching between divergent and convergent thinking, try Invergent, an experimental, browser-based thinking toolkit designed to help users deliberately move between exploring possibilities and making decisions.

It combines divergent thinking to expand the possibility space, convergent thinking to evaluate options using constraints and trade-offs, and switching exercises to practice moving between exploration and selection. Its lightweight, data-driven design uses an editable JSON question bank, heuristic profiles, and timed learning sessions to support reflection and practice.

Treat it as a practice tool, not a validated clinical assessment or a guarantee of increased intelligence. Its value comes from the quality of the questions, your effort, and what you learn from reflecting on your answers.

5. Third Principle: Do Not Confuse Information with Learning

Modern life makes it easy to collect links, save videos, highlight passages, and accumulate notes. These activities can be useful, but they do not prove that learning has occurred.

Learning is more convincing when you can retrieve an idea without looking, explain it in your own words, apply it to a new problem, or notice when it does not fit the evidence.

A major review by Dunlosky and colleagues evaluated ten common learning techniques. It found strong support for practice testing and distributed practice, while techniques such as rereading and highlighting alone often had lower utility when used as primary strategies. A later review in Nature Reviews Psychology also emphasizes the benefits of spacing learning over time and retrieving information from memory.

Sources: Dunlosky et al. (2013), Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques; Carpenter, Pan & Butler (2022), The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice.

Retrieve

Close the source and write down what you remember. Then compare your recall with the original and correct the gaps.

Space

Return to important material over multiple sessions rather than trying to absorb everything in one marathon session.

Explain

Ask “why?” and “how?” Connect a new idea to examples, mechanisms, counterexamples, and concepts you already understand.

Apply

Use the concept in a real task, a worked example, a small experiment, or a problem that differs from the original example.

For example, after reading about cognitive flexibility, do not stop at underlining the definition. Put the source away and explain what it means. Then identify an occasion when you changed your mind because of new evidence, and another occasion when you should have considered more alternatives.

That process turns reading into retrieval, explanation, and application. It also exposes the difference between familiarity—“I have seen this before”—and actual recall.

6. Fourth Principle: Practice Deliberately, Not Merely Frequently

The cultivator metaphor is especially useful here. Repeating an activity can improve performance, but repetition alone is not a magic formula. Practice becomes more informative when it targets a specific skill, includes feedback, and gives you a chance to correct errors.

Research on expert performance has examined the role of deliberate practice: structured activities designed to improve performance, often involving effortful work on weaknesses and informative feedback. The details vary by domain, and practice is not the only factor behind expertise. Access to instruction, prior knowledge, motivation, opportunity, health, and other circumstances also matter.

Further reading: Ericsson et al. (1993), The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance; Ericsson & Harwell (2019), Deliberate Practice and Proposed Limits on the Effects of Practice.

Instead of saying, “I will become better at thinking,” choose a specific practice target:

  • Critical reading: distinguish a source’s evidence from its interpretation and conclusion.
  • Systems thinking: map the actors, incentives, dependencies, feedback loops, and unintended consequences in a problem.
  • Programming: build a small feature, test it, inspect failure cases, and document what the debugging process taught you.
  • Writing: explain a complex concept to a beginner, revise the explanation, and remove claims that are unclear or unsupported.
  • Decision-making: record your assumptions, expected outcomes, uncertainties, and the evidence that would change your mind.

Use a feedback loop: choose one target, practice it, review the result, identify the most important error, and practice again. Keep the challenge demanding enough to reveal weaknesses but manageable enough that you can learn from them.

7. Fifth Principle: Develop Metacognition—Learn How You Learn

A modern sage needs to think about thinking. Metacognition includes awareness of your own knowledge and the ability to regulate your learning: planning, monitoring understanding, and evaluating what worked.

It is easy to mistake confidence for competence. A passage may feel obvious while you read it, yet become difficult to explain once the page is closed. A useful safeguard is to compare your confidence with observable performance.

Before learning: What do I already know, and what question am I trying to answer?

During learning: Can I explain the mechanism, or am I only recognizing the words?

After learning: Can I retrieve the main idea, apply it, and name what remains uncertain?

Later: What do I still remember, and what needs another practice session?

Keep a small learning log. It does not need to be elaborate. Record the question, the source, the main idea in your own words, one practical application, one unresolved question, and what you will revisit later.

This habit also helps protect against overconfidence. A thoughtful learner is not someone who doubts everything; it is someone who can distinguish what is known, what is inferred, what is uncertain, and what evidence could change the conclusion.

8. Sixth Principle: Use Writing to Organize and Retain Ideas

Writing is not merely a way to display knowledge. It can be a tool for discovering whether an idea is coherent. When you explain a concept to another person, you must choose a structure, make hidden assumptions visible, connect evidence to claims, and identify gaps in your own understanding.

Try the “one idea, three layers” method:

  1. Simple explanation: describe the idea in plain language.
  2. Mechanism: explain why or how it works, with evidence where available.
  3. Application and limitation: give an example, a counterexample, and a condition under which the idea might not apply.

Stories can also help organize concepts into meaningful sequences, but a memorable story is not automatically accurate. Keep the narrative connected to evidence and distinguish a helpful analogy from a proven mechanism.

Want to learn more effectively? Read this companion article about storytelling, memory, and long-term retention.

Explore Better Memory & Retention →

9. Seventh Principle: Build a Personal Knowledge System

Ancient scrolls, libraries, notebooks, scientific journals, code repositories, and digital databases can all serve a similar purpose: preserving knowledge so it can be revisited, compared, tested, and applied.

A personal knowledge system does not need to become a complicated productivity project. Start with a simple structure:

Questions

Keep a list of questions worth investigating. Good questions help you avoid collecting information without a purpose.

Sources

Save the original source, author, date, and relevant context. Prefer primary evidence and reputable reviews where appropriate.

Insights

Write your interpretation separately from the source’s claim. Note supporting evidence, limitations, and competing explanations.

Experiments

Record what you tried, what happened, what failed, and what you would change next time.

Use technology to reduce friction, not to create the illusion of productivity. A beautifully organized archive is not useful if you never retrieve or apply its contents.

Review your notes periodically. Ask whether each item still matters, whether your understanding has changed, and whether two ideas can be connected. Knowledge becomes more useful when it can be retrieved and adapted to a new context.

10. Eighth Principle: Protect Depth Without Rejecting the World

The hermit is a metaphor for deliberate distance, not necessarily permanent withdrawal from society. Other people can challenge assumptions, offer feedback, reveal blind spots, and expose us to experiences that solitary study cannot provide.

A balanced modern practice combines focused solitude with deliberate engagement:

  • Spend some time learning without notifications or unnecessary interruptions.
  • Discuss important ideas with people who can challenge them respectfully.
  • Seek criticism that helps improve the work, not only praise that confirms your beliefs.
  • Take breaks and protect sleep; attention and learning are not improved simply by pushing harder without limit.
  • Return to real-world problems to test whether your understanding actually helps.

Emotional discipline should not become emotional suppression, and solitude should not become avoidance. If a difficult feeling or situation needs conversation, support, or practical action, retreating indefinitely may not solve it.

The point is not to escape the world forever. It is to engage with the world more intentionally, with a mind that is less easily pulled in every direction.

11. A Practical 30-Day Modern Sage Experiment

A practical roadmap: turn the metaphor into repeatable habits.

You do not need to wait for perfect conditions. Treat the next 30 days as an experiment in attention, learning, and practice—not a guaranteed brain transformation or a test of personal worth.

Days 1–7: Observe and clear

Notice your biggest sources of distraction. Choose one daily focus block. Write down one question you genuinely want to understand.

Days 8–14: Learn actively

Study one topic using reliable sources. After each session, retrieve the main points from memory and explain them in your own words.

Days 15–21: Generate and evaluate

Use divergent thinking to create several approaches to one problem. Then use convergent thinking to compare evidence, constraints, and trade-offs.

Days 22–30: Practice and integrate

Build a small output: an essay, prototype, map, analysis, lesson, or solution. Seek feedback, revise it, and record what the process taught you.

At the end of each week, ask yourself:

  • What can I now explain or do that I could not do before?
  • What did I retrieve from memory without looking at my notes?
  • Which assumption changed because of new evidence?
  • What mistake taught me the most?
  • What is the next specific skill I should practice?

Keep the routine realistic. A shorter session that you can sustain may be more useful than an ambitious schedule that collapses after three days. Adjust the experiment to your responsibilities, energy, and circumstances.

12. What a Modern-Day Great Sage Is—and Is Not

A modern sage is...

  • Curious but willing to question assumptions.
  • Disciplined but capable of changing methods.
  • Ambitious without being ruled by comparison.
  • Knowledgeable while honest about uncertainty.
  • Willing to practice, fail, receive feedback, and revise.

A modern sage is not...

  • A person who knows everything.
  • Someone who avoids all emotion or relationships.
  • A person who consumes endless information without applying it.
  • Someone who mistakes confidence for evidence.
  • A person who believes one routine works for everyone.

Wisdom includes knowing when to act, when to wait, when to ask for help, when to change your mind, and when the available evidence is not enough to justify certainty.

Expertise is usually domain-specific: being excellent at one task does not automatically make someone wise in every other area. The aim is not to become a superhuman who can solve everything, but to build transferable habits of attention, learning, reasoning, and self-correction.

13. The Deeper Meaning of Cultivation

Return to the ancient images: the hermit on a mountain, the cultivator training alone, the scholar studying scrolls, and the sage who eventually acts with extraordinary clarity.

We can read these images as a sequence of questions for modern life:

  • The Hermit asks: What deserves my attention—and what is merely consuming it?
  • The Cultivator asks: Which ability am I building through deliberate practice?
  • The Scholar asks: What do I actually know, and how do I know it?
  • The Great Sage asks: Given what I know, what is the wisest action in this context?

In this interpretation, the scroll may be a scientific paper, a technical manual, a history book, or a carefully documented experiment. The mountain may be a quiet room, a library, a workshop, or an uninterrupted hour away from a feed. Cultivation may be writing, coding, researching, teaching, repairing, designing, or practicing a difficult skill.

The external symbols change. The deeper discipline remains: create space to think, learn what matters, practice what you learn, test it against reality, and revise your understanding when reality disagrees.

The modern Great Sage hypothesis:

A Great Sage is not merely someone who empties the mind, but someone who deliberately withdraws from unnecessary distractions and worldly attachments to cultivate knowledge, discipline, skills, and wisdom.

Do not simply consume more information. Learn to ask better questions, generate more possibilities, evaluate them carefully, practice deliberately, and use what you learn with humility.

Perhaps the real cultivation is this: stop letting every signal command your attention, and start deciding what kind of mind you want to build.

title: Why Effort Changes the Opportunity to Solve a Problem: Samsung, Nokia, and the Psychology of Repair
author: Angga Conni Saputra
excerpt: Effort does not guarantee success, but relevant and sustained effort can create opportunities to diagnose problems, reduce harm, rebuild trust, and adapt. Explore the Samsung Galaxy Note7 recall, Nokia's smartphone decline, and the psychology of effective repair.
content:
Psychology • Strategy • Conflict Repair • Systems Thinking

Effort does not guarantee success. But relevant, sustained effort can change what is possible: it creates more opportunities to understand a problem, test solutions, reduce harm, and rebuild trust.

When a conflict remains unresolved, people sometimes say, “If it is meant to be, things will work out,” or “Time will heal everything.” Those statements may offer comfort, but they can also hide an important question: what is anyone actually doing to make a better outcome possible?

Problems do not all require the same response. A small misunderstanding may need one honest conversation. A serious breach of trust may require accountability, repeated evidence of change, and time. The size and nature of the damage should shape the kind of effort used to repair it.

Effort matters not because suffering proves sincerity, but because meaningful action can create opportunities that passive waiting leaves unused.

1. Effort changes the opportunity—not the guarantee

Imagine a conflict as a situation with several possible paths. One path is avoidance: do nothing, hope emotions fade, and assume the other person will eventually move on. Another is repair: clarify what happened, listen to the impact, accept responsibility, propose a relevant remedy, and follow through.

Repair does not guarantee reconciliation. The other person may still decline to continue the relationship, and that choice must be respected. Yet active repair can create opportunities that did not exist before: an opportunity to correct misinformation, understand the harm, demonstrate accountability, or make an informed decision about the future.

Low or misdirected effortLeaves important questions unanswered, relies on assumptions, and may allow avoidable damage to continue.
Relevant, sustained effortCreates more chances to learn what went wrong, test a remedy, respond to feedback, and show that change is real.
OutcomeStill depends on many factors: the severity of harm, timing, context, the quality of the response, and whether both people want to participate.

2. Interactive model: how effort can change the opportunity for repair

Select each stage in the diagram. Notice that effort does not magically jump straight to forgiveness. It creates intermediate opportunities, and each one can succeed or fail.

Selected: Conflict. Effort begins by acknowledging that something needs attention.

This diagram is a conceptual model for reflection, not a validated mathematical formula or a guarantee of a particular outcome.

3. Case study: Samsung Galaxy Note7—accepting a costly remedy

In 2016, Samsung's Galaxy Note7 phones were found to have a battery-related fire hazard. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission's recall notice described risks of overheating and catching fire, and offered consumers a refund or replacement remedy. Samsung announced that it had stopped sales and would voluntarily replace devices, then worked with regulators and retail partners on the recall process.

In the United States, Samsung's exchange program offered customers choices that included exchanging the Note7 for a Galaxy S7 or S7 edge, with a refund of the price difference, or taking part in the replacement process. When replacement devices also presented safety concerns, Samsung stopped production and sales and expanded the recall to include both original and replacement devices.

That is a useful example of costly corrective action. A company could not responsibly solve a safety problem with a reassuring slogan alone. It needed to stop sales, coordinate logistics, give customers a practical remedy, investigate the failure, and accept commercial consequences.

What the example shows: the company created a more credible path to consumer protection by taking concrete action, not merely by saying that customer safety mattered.

Samsung's response was not flawless, and the replacement-device problem showed that the first corrective action was insufficient. This makes the case more instructive, not less: effort must include learning and adjustment. A costly first response is not enough if evidence shows that the underlying risk remains.

Samsung's 2017 sustainability report later described extensive investigation, including testing more than 200,000 devices and 30,000 batteries, and said it had worked to identify the causes of the battery failures. These figures are reported by Samsung itself, so they should be understood as the company's account of its investigation.

The lesson is not that every organisation should always choose the most expensive response. The lesson is that when the potential harm is serious, a proportionate response may require accepting substantial cost to protect people and address the damage.

4. The contrasting case: Nokia and the cost of a delayed strategic response

Nokia is often described as a company that “ignored customers” or simply refused to innovate. That is too simplistic. Its decline in the smartphone market had multiple causes, including organisational conflict, strategic decisions, a fragmented software environment, and the industry's shift from hardware-led competition toward operating systems, apps, and platform ecosystems.

Research discussed by INSEAD notes that Nokia was initially dismissive of the iPhone and Android challenge while its Symbian operating system was ageing and its app ecosystem struggled to match competitors. A separate study of Nokia's decline describes how organisational design and strategic choices made it harder for the company to respond effectively to the transition.

Nokia did try to respond, including through its Windows Phone partnership with Microsoft. But effort is not automatically effective just because an organisation is busy. If a response arrives late, relies on risky assumptions, or does not meet what users and developers need, it may fail to recover the opportunity that has already shifted elsewhere.

Important correction: Nokia did not simply “go bankrupt.” Its handset business was sold to Microsoft; Nokia continued as a company and focused more heavily on network infrastructure and other businesses. The more accurate lesson is that it lost its former dominance in mobile phones, not that the entire company disappeared.

This contrasts with the Note7 recall in a useful way. Samsung's safety crisis demanded immediate corrective action to reduce direct harm. Nokia's platform crisis demanded earlier strategic adaptation, stronger software execution, and a more effective response to a changing ecosystem. Different problems require different kinds of effort.

5. Why effort can change the odds: five mechanisms

It improves diagnosis.
Effort spent listening, investigating, and checking evidence reduces the chance of solving the wrong problem.
It creates options.
People who explore alternatives can discover routes that passive waiting never reveals.
It reduces ongoing harm.
In safety or trust crises, timely action can limit further damage while a fuller solution is developed.
It creates observable evidence.
Promises describe intentions. Actions and follow-through give others evidence to evaluate.
It enables adaptation.
When the first attempt fails, feedback and continued work make correction possible.

These mechanisms explain why effort can improve the probability of an effective solution. They do not mean that effort alone controls outcomes. A well-executed plan can still fail because of external constraints, insufficient resources, incompatible goals, or damage that cannot be reversed.

6. Effort must match the damage—and the actual problem

Consider three examples:

A misunderstandingRelevant effort might mean clarifying what was said, listening without interruption, and correcting a false assumption.
A breach of trustRelevant effort might mean admitting what happened, answering reasonable questions, changing the behavior, and remaining consistent over time.
A product safety failureRelevant effort may require stopping sales, recalling the product, providing refunds or replacements, investigating the cause, and preventing recurrence.

Notice that the amount of effort is not the only issue. Its direction matters. An expensive gift may do little to repair a repeated breach of trust. A public apology may do little to protect consumers if the dangerous product remains in circulation.

The right question is not simply “How much effort was made?” It is “Was the effort proportionate to the harm, directed at the real cause, and sustained long enough to make a difference?”

7. A practical framework for evaluating effort

Use these questions when assessing a conflict, a project failure, a customer complaint, or an organisational crisis:

What exactly was damaged?
Identify the harm, its scale, who experienced it, and whether it is continuing.
Who has responsibility to act?
Separate the responsibility to repair harm from the separate question of whether the affected person chooses to forgive or continue.
What action would address the cause?
Choose a remedy that fits the actual problem rather than a symbolic gesture that merely looks impressive.
What obstacles are real?
Account for safety, resources, time, access, and other constraints. Look for reasonable alternatives rather than demanding reckless sacrifice.
What evidence would show progress?
Define observable signs: a corrected process, a kept commitment, fewer repeat incidents, clearer communication, or improved user outcomes.
What happens if the first attempt fails?
Review the evidence, acknowledge shortcomings, and adapt the response. Do not assume that good intentions make an ineffective remedy sufficient.

8. In relationships, effort is not a test of suffering

There is a risk in talking about effort: people may interpret it as a demand to prove love through dramatic gestures, unlimited availability, or unsafe sacrifices. That is not the point.

Showing up uninvited, lying to provoke a reaction, manufacturing an emergency, or ignoring someone's boundaries is not a healthy way to measure care. These behaviours can create pressure and confusion rather than genuine repair.

More useful evidence includes whether someone takes initiative, communicates honestly, makes realistic plans, follows through, accepts responsibility, and changes the behaviour that caused the problem. If circumstances prevent a planned action, proposing a reasonable alternative can also show commitment.

And the person who was hurt retains the right to say no. Effort can create an opportunity for repair; it does not create an entitlement to forgiveness, access, or reconciliation.

Conclusion: Effort changes what becomes possible

The Samsung Note7 case illustrates how a company can respond to a serious product safety problem with costly corrective action. Nokia's smartphone decline illustrates a different risk: when a changing environment demands a timely and effective strategic response, fragmented or poorly aligned decisions can allow an opportunity to disappear. Neither case is a simple morality tale, and neither proves that effort guarantees success.

Together, they point to a broader principle. Effective effort creates opportunities to diagnose, act, learn, and adapt. Insufficient or misdirected effort can leave problems unresolved or allow them to grow. The key is not effort for its own sake, but effort that matches the scale and nature of the problem.

Time does not recall a product. Good intentions do not fix a broken process. And wanting a relationship to heal does not, by itself, rebuild trust. Meaningful effort is the bridge between recognising a problem and creating a real opportunity to solve it.

This article uses business cases as illustrations of a general problem-solving principle. Corporate outcomes have multiple causes; the cases should not be interpreted as proof that effort alone caused success or failure.
